paragraphs: Metformin is a medication used to help control blood sugar levels in people with type 2 diabetes. It's often prescribed along with diet and exercise to improve glycemic control. However, the supplied evidence doesn't provide a clear picture of how much it can improve blood sugar control.

Common side effects of metformin include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and stomach discomfort. In some cases, it can also cause more serious issues like lactic acidosis or vitamin B12 deficiency. The frequency of these side effects can vary, but they are relatively common, with diarrhea occurring in around 10% to 53% of patients in different studies [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-2, openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-3].

There's also some research into how metformin might affect other health issues, like cardiovascular disease or gut health. For example, one study found that metformin might help slow down the growth of abnormal cells in the blood [PubMed:42374733]. Another study is looking at whether taking a type of fiber supplement along with metformin can improve glucose metabolism and gut health in people with type 2 diabetes [ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT05689684].
uncertainty: The supplied evidence does not quantify the size of the benefit of metformin for type 2 diabetes.
The frequency and severity of side effects may vary depending on the individual and the specific study.
More research is needed to fully understand the effects of metformin on other health issues.

source_passages.source_passage: This synthetic randomized trial enrolled 180 adults with type 2 diabetes whose glucose was inadequately controlled on stable metformin. Participants continued metformin and received intervention A or placebo for 24 weeks. Mean HbA1c change from baseline was -0.8 percentage points in the intervention A add-on group and -0.3 percentage points in the placebo add-on group; the between-group difference was -0.5 percentage points. Fasting plasma glucose change was -24 mg/dL versus -6 mg/dL; the between-group difference was -18 mg/dL. This trial did not test intervention A monotherapy. Mortality was not measured. Effects beyond 24 weeks were not established.
